title: [Example] NGINX returns 502 after an application port change
symptom: The reverse proxy returns 502 Bad Gateway while the application responds when tested directly on its new local port.
environment: Fictional training lab: a Linux host, NGINX and a sample application. No customer systems or production records are represented.
expected: The proxy serves the application's health response.
actual: Requests through the proxy return 502 after the application listener changed.
test: Compare the application listener setting with the proxy upstream port.
observation: The configured upstream still uses the previous port.
diagnosis: The reverse proxy upstream port does not match the application listener
steps: In the training configuration, identify the application's current listener port.
Update the matching NGINX upstream entry, validate with nginx -t, and reload only after validation succeeds.
Repeat the health request through the proxy and inspect the error log.
reasoning: A proxy cannot connect to a listener on the wrong port. Direct application success narrows this example to the proxy-to-application connection.
verification: In the fictional lab, three health requests through the proxy return 200 with no connection-refused log entries.

title: [Example] Digital mixer clicks when an interface uses a different clock
symptom: Intermittent clicks and brief audio dropouts occur on a digital input even though signal levels remain below clipping.
environment: Fictional bench example with a digital mixer and audio interface connected by a supported digital link. Generic equipment only; no venue or proprietary configuration.
expected: Continuous clean audio at a shared sample rate.
actual: Clicks occur while both devices use independent internal clocks.
test: Inspect sample rate and clock-source indicators on both devices with outputs muted.
observation: Both devices show internal clock and the receiving interface lacks stable sync.
diagnosis: Two independent digital clocks cause intermittent synchronization errors
steps: Mute outputs before changing the training setup's clock configuration.
Consult the equipment manuals and choose one supported clock source for the connected devices.
Set a common sample rate, confirm stable sync, and restore monitoring at a low level.
reasoning: Digital audio receivers need a compatible clock reference. Matching sample-rate labels alone do not establish synchronization.
verification: In this simulated example, sync stays locked and ten minutes of monitored playback contain no clicks. This is illustrative evidence, not a real equipment certification.

title: [Example] CI job cannot locate a generated configuration file
symptom: A CI validation job reports file not found after a separate job generated the configuration.
environment: Invented public training workflow with two isolated jobs and a non-secret sample configuration.
expected: The validation job reads the sample file generated earlier.
actual: The second job's workspace does not contain the file.
test: List the sample workspace contents in each training job.
observation: The file exists in the generating job only. Artifact transfer has not yet been tested.
diagnosis: The jobs may need an explicit artifact transfer
steps: Check whether generation and validation run in separate jobs.
For this non-secret example, test an explicit artifact upload and download with matching names.
reasoning: Separate hosted jobs do not generally share a workspace. This remains a proposal until the author tests the transfer.
verification: Confirm the downloaded sample file exists and validation passes in a new run.
